I have been keeping this for you: {0}. Have you made room this time?
So this is what you look like. She described you completely wrong.
Want to hear what she said? Not telling. You'd get smug.
She used to ask me which dress to wear before going out. Now she won't even take the job I found her.
...Never mind. I'll tell her that myself.
The goods really are for sale. I also wanted to see whether you'd take a bargain that walked in the door.
Done. Don't tell her about this. She'd definitely call me a busybody.
I've seen that pattern on her bracelet box in upper-district catalogs.
It's her family's. They're one of the upper-district houses selling household goods, perfume and fabric.
When she was little, shop assistants asked whether she liked something before she even looked at the price. Here, she wanted to see what happens when no one flatters her.
Her family sells perfume and bedding. They can't influence the courts. All she can do is come down every few days to see me. Of all her friends upstairs, she's the only one left.
She cares. She just always wants to pick the whole road for me.
The two walk up to the window one after the other. Eleanor scans the shelves through the frame.
I said I'd bring you today. Kept my word, didn't I?
All I heard the whole way was you nagging.
You're the one who grabbed your bag and left before me.
I was heading out to buy things anyway.
Sure, sure. "Anyway" right up to his counter.
So the shop you always talk about is this tiny.
Talking at the window feels like shouting in someone's ear.
...Wait, am I being too loud?
You're only noticing now?
So what am I supposed to do here?
Sit.
But there's only one old stool by the window.
And the other one's piled with your stock.
He gave you the stool. Just sit.
On the second shelf sits an old brass watch whose lid won't quite close.
Were all these old things on the shelves pawned?
Mostly.
And if nobody redeems them, they just stay here?
People need money to get by.
Can I see that old brass watch on the second shelf?
(Holding the brass watch in both hands) It's heavier than it looks.
What's this black grime in the lid's seam that won't wipe off?
Ore dust.
There's a name engraved inside, too. The edges are worn smooth.
Will you sell this watch?
Not to you.
Why not? It's not like I'd pay less.
You'd only buy it as a conversation piece.
Then lock it in a glass case the moment you got home.
He's not wrong. She really would.
This watch isn't for sale.
Hey, I haven't even said I'd buy it!
Can't I even take a look through the window?
Once you've had your look, your next line's the price.
The old brass watch goes into the drawer under the counter.
I only pointed at it. Why'd you put it away?
He's afraid you'll start throwing money at him.
What on earth do you two think I am?
Anyway, I came here on real business today.
(Biting her pen cap, flipping open a notebook) I made a list for Eleanor.
First, two crates of long-lasting Nutrifruit delivered to her place.
Then four thick blankets. The nights are freezing.
And the stairs in your building—why isn't there a single light?
Lydia, put your pen down.
Don't send it to her place.
Even you're stopping me? It's not like I'm wasting money.
Two crates of Nutrifruit at her door would stand out.
By tomorrow the whole building would know whose gift she took.
If she needs something, ask her yourself.
...Fine. I didn't think it through.
Lydia closes her little notebook and tucks it back into her shoulder bag.
The stairwell needs a lamp at least, plus some spare bulbs.
List twenty things if you like. None of it's coming into my room.
If you won't let the delivery people in, I'll carry it up myself.
If it doesn't fit in one trip, I'll make three.
The little notebook is passed through the window and lands on the counter.
None of this needs delivering.
What about the stuff on the second half of the page?
Don't stock it.
How are you even harder to talk to than Eleanor?
Then no crates. I'll find out what it takes to fix the stairwell light.
Someone at the ration station or on the street must handle that, right?
...Suit yourself. Just don't let anyone fleece you.
Fine. I won't stop you on the light.
Then it's settled. I'm coming back to sit here a whole afternoon.
There's only one stool by the window.
There's another inside.
Another wooden stool is dragged out from under the counter and passed through the window, next to the old one.
The wood's rock-hard, but I'll call it thoughtful.
Move your bag. You're taking up my spot.
Lydia comes in with both hands empty, bag strap wound twice around her wrist.
See? Empty hands.
Before I left, I turned my bag upside down and shook it three times.
Sit.
I got to the bottom of the light thing.
The ration station sent me to Housing, Housing sent me to the street office, and the street office told me to find Old Zhou, the repairman.
Three places, three faces, all saying the same thing: not my problem.
Up there, I never had to run around for a single light.
Up there, if a light broke, someone came to replace it the next day.
Old Zhou says he has wire, but no bulbs.
I've got a box here.
You—
You could've said that sooner.
You just asked.
How much?
Three each. Six in the box. Pick out the bad ones.
You even pick through them.
Put a bad one in, Old Zhou has to climb up again.
Then I'll wait till you're done picking.
She drags the stool half a foot closer, sits, and puts both hands on her knees.
I came today because I wanted to say—
The door is shoved open. Two men come in one after the other. The one in front takes off his hat.
Boss.
You buy things?
I buy.
Then her stuff—you buy that too?
His eyes land on Lydia's wrist and stay there.
I've got nothing to sell.
The thing on your hand.
That's not for sale.
Don't sell, then.
Then we settle another bill.
New face on this street. Twenty a month.
Twenty credits.
Twenty.
You know what twenty credits buys up there?
No.
Tell me.
He steps half a pace closer, hand on the counter edge, one finger from the bracelet.
The shopkeeper comes around from behind the counter and stands between them.
Hands off.
Who are you.
The shopkeeper.
Good. Your shop goes on the bill too.
How much.
Fifty.
My shop doesn't bring in fifty a month.
Then pay in goods.
All right.
...All right?
In the counter: six bulbs, a comb missing three teeth, half a can of nails.
You carry it.
You think I'm here to beg?
I'm talking business.
You want money, I don't have it. You want goods, I'll weigh them for you.
He actually has a scale.
Shut up.
What are you selling?
I'm not selling anything.
Then you're standing in the wrong place.
This shop's just business.
...You're talking business to me.
He's telling you the rules.
What're rules worth?
He tosses his hat onto the counter and reaches out a hand.
The shopkeeper goes around and pulls the door wide, letting the alley light in.
Outside.
So I can't even come in and sit?
Not doing business with you.
Not many on this street say no to business.
Now there's one more.
He pushes the door back.
Then I'm buying anyway.
His hand comes down and grabs the wrist with the bracelet.
Let go.
Bracelet stays with me. Go get the money.
The pen tip stabs into the back of his hand. She steps forward with it.
He jerks his hand back, backs to the door, and crushes his hat.
You—
I'm counting to three.
One.
This street's only so long.
You go to the end, you still gotta come back.
The door slams. The glass shakes twice before it stops.
...The pen's bent.
I stabbed him pretty hard, didn't I?
His hand was all black. Did the pen leak?
It's blood.
She sets the pen on the counter and wipes her fingertips twice on her pant seam.
I wasn't scared at all back there.
Starting to be now.
Scared? Sit a minute.
They know my bracelet.
Last time I walked this whole street wearing it.
I even stopped at the corner and watched the fuss for ages.
There's no fuss on this street.
...Then I remembered wrong.
I was thinking about something else.
Twenty isn't after you.
Then who?
The street. New faces are easy to squeeze.
So coming empty-handed was a mistake too.
You came.
...That sounded like a compliment.
It's the truth.
I'm still buying the bulbs. All six. Broken ones too.
Broken ones are useless.
I'll take them to Old Zhou. Show him how difficult I can be.
She counts the money onto the counter, bill by bill. Then pushes it over. Not far.
Can you walk me out?
Just to the corner.
I can.
He sweeps the counter into the drawer. Presses the lock twice.
Across the alley, someone leans against the wall. Sees them come out. Turns and walks away.
That person...
Saw them.
Here's far enough.
I know the way.
She walks a dozen steps, glances back once, then turns the corner.
Eleanor sets the cloth bag on the corner of the counter. Two lengths of copper pipe stick out of the top.
Weigh it.
Where's it from?
Behind Building Seven. Old pipes. The old man at the gate nodded.
He stood there watching while I pulled them out. Didn't say no.
Copper. Three pounds two.
What's it worth?
Thirty-five.
Last time, pipes like these, you gave me twenty.
Last time that piece was packed with cement.
They could name that number. Means they already asked.
Asked which building I live in. How many people in my family.
They asked what this shop can pay.
Same thing.
…I knocked on these ones.
Knocked on, it's thirty-five.
Lydia stands by the door, a paper box under her arm, eyes on the alley.
She's been at the door a quarter hour.
Saw her.
She says someone on this street is watching her bracelet.
Her hands shook the whole time she said it. Then she laughed.
What'd you come here for today?
I came to settle the bulb bill.
And to see if that bar's still behind your door.
It is.
Then I'll sit a while longer.
Six men come in from the alley mouth. Not fast. They fill the doorway.
Boss.
The one who stuck me last time. Still here?
Still here.
I wasn't asking you.
I answered anyway.
He laughs once.
Today it's not about twenty.
Two thousand.
Two thousand for what?
Two people.
You're kidnapping people.
I said please.
What's that in your hand?
A coil of rope hangs by his hand, its end dragging on the floor.
People upstairs pay two thousand for a daughter. Not hard.
Or they don't pay. She comes with us first. Family will come around.
The men who took my mother said the same thing.
Say a name first. Then please.
Who's your mother?
None of your business.
They're not going out that door.
You don't get a say.
Two men move around both sides of the counter and block the way inside.
A hand shoves the shelf; shelf and goods spill outward.
The shopkeeper's back hits the counter corner; forehead cracks against the iron band on the beam.
Hands off!
She yanks the wooden bar from behind the door and jams one end into the man's ribs.
Take the bar.
Two hands wrench the bar away. She's pulled into the doorframe and lands on her shoulder.
Lydia—the door!
Lydia pulls the door open and shouts twice into the alley.
At both ends of the alley, roller shutters clatter up one after another.
He grabs the old watch from the shelf.
Go.
A foot stamps down under the shelf; an empty blood bag splits open.
Footsteps run off down the alley. The shutters drop back down.
Your head.
Door first.
The door's crooked.
Crooked can be fixed.
Your forehead's dripping.
I'll sweep the floor.
Loudspeaker at the alley mouth: No loitering in groups on this street after dark. Violators will be registered.
Lydia comes back from the alley, holding a paper with two lines written on it.
I asked at three places.
Two wouldn't open. One did—an old lady.
She said this bunch took a kid from over by the docks last month.
The family scraped the money together. The kid was back on the third day.
When she said it, the door was only open a crack.
Halfway through, she told me to stop asking.
What's on the paper.
What she said.
I was afraid I'd get it wrong.
She slaps the paper on the counter.
I'm going to the Watch office tomorrow.
The Watch charges a filing fee.
I'll pay.
I can't afford to owe you that favor.
What's that got to do with favors?
You pay, and this becomes your business.
It was my business to begin with!
...It was my bracelet they were looking at.
If I'd taken it off and tucked it in my sleeve, none of this would've happened that day.
Last time I stood right here and laughed about your place having no windows.
While I was laughing, they were probably crouched at the alley mouth watching me.
They didn't start crouching there today.
You knew?
I knew someone was watching. Didn't know there were six.
Then why didn't you say so?
You wouldn't have come.
You're right. I wouldn't have.
So you'd rather I take that hit.
I'd rather have you mad at me.
Eleanor found a wet cloth in the back and pressed it to the side of his forehead.
Two thousand.
Go report it. Come back after.
You're not stopping me.
Can't.
She went out. Came back half an hour later, paper still in her hand.
The window said I need a registration. And a witness.
Witness has to be from this street.
Nobody on this street will sign.
The shopkeeper crouched down and stacked the old goods scattered on the floor back into the box, one by one.
The report can wait till tomorrow.
Tomorrow they might be here.
Then we deal with it tomorrow.
Now pick this up.
What's the point of picking it up.
We open in the morning.
She crouched down, picked up the blood bag cracked underfoot first, and shook it twice.
Can this still be sold?
Can't take it.
Then what if he comes to redeem it?
He won't.
How do you know.
If he were coming, he'd be here already.
She rolls up the blood bag, into a ball, and holds it down with both hands.
I'll bring two hundred tomorrow.
Don't.
It's not for you.
I'm the one who wrecked this room. I pay.
Two hundred won't cover the watch.
...That watch is expensive?
It's collateral.
Then just sell the collateral and be done.
I don't sell collateral.
She stands up.
Fine. Then name a number.
Not now.
You're something.
You won't even let me feel bad about it.
She folds the paper twice, holds it, and steps into the light at the door.
Put the bracelet away. Don't wear it on this street.
So you think I brought them here too.
I'm saying don't let anyone see it.
She slips the bracelet off, holds it a moment, and shoves it in her pocket.
When I wear it, I feel like it's my grandmother's.
The hinge is off half an inch. The door won't shut. Wind comes through the gap.
Eleanor pulls the cloth away and looks.
Not deep.
It'll scar.
Let it scar.
You're awfully agreeable.
That last one was two fingers off. You'd have lost that eye.
It wasn't off.
That's luck, not skill.
You didn't even have an iron bar, and you stood in the middle.
I had the counter.
The counter fell.
Fell or not, it's still there.
And the watch?
It was taken.
Pawned?
Pawned.
How long has it been pawned?
A year and three months.
If he doesn't come to redeem it, it's yours.
He came by last month.
…He came?
Stood at the door. Didn't come in.
Asked for two more months.
What did you say?
I said it was here.
It's not here now.
I'll go find it.
Find who?
That alley.
You're going alone.
Alone.
You're going with all that blood on your head.
Six of them. They know your face.
They know the counter.
You're a counter too?
Something like that.
She presses the cloth back down. A little harder.
Sit.
I'm fine standing.
Sit. Blood's running down your neck.
He sits. The stool leg scrapes on the brick.
I read something in a book once. That people go lightheaded at a time like this.
You don't look it.
Going lightheaded wouldn't help.
You'd still do it.
The day they took my mother, I stood in the doorway till dark.
I couldn't do anything then.
Today I pushed back at him.
Not well. He took it off me.
You landed it.
...I landed it.
He flinched. I saw it.
Lydia comes back from the door, sets the hammer on the counter. Dust on her palm.
Door nailed shut?
Two boards.
It has to open tomorrow.
We'll see when it opens.
She pulls the paper out of her pocket, puts it on the counter, flattens it.
I'll hold on to the paper.
That's my writing on it.
I know.
I'll come early tomorrow.
Suit yourself.
Not suit yourself. I'm doing it.
She folds the paper, tucks it in her pocket, and lifts the crooked door back up.
This door won't sit straight anymore.
It blocks the wind.
It won't block people.
Daybreak. Eleanor stands outside the door. A tool bag at her feet. A screwdriver and two screws in her hand.
You said come early. So I came early.
I didn't say that.
I said it. Same thing.
Found these under your counter. Don't charge me.
They were mine to begin with.
That's why I'm not charging.
The shopkeeper holds the door panel up. She crouches and turns the screws. The screwdriver slips twice.
These screw heads are stripped. Who put these in.
Me.
...Fine. It's holding, at least.
A little higher. Good. Hold still.
The last turn goes tight. The door closes to a crack. She puts the screwdriver back in the bag and grips it by the top.
It'll close now.
Your forehead's not even scabbed over. Don't lift so hard.
The door's heavier than my head.
Hah. You'll compare anything.
Hey.
That day, after they got the bar out of my hands—
I thought the next one was landing on me.
It didn't. You stepped in front.
The counter was right there.
Cut it out. The counter went down. You stayed standing.
Growing up, no one stood in front of me like that. Except my mother.
The people above us just say "don't be scared, miss," and step back.
You say nothing. You step forward.
You. You're solid.
I... like you. That's all.
The shopkeeper sets down the screw box and stands.
Eleanor—
Eleanor.
Saying my name doesn't work either. I wasn't done— no. I'm done.
The shopkeeper pours a cup of water and pushes it over. She stares at the rim. Doesn't take it.
That's your answer? Ridiculous.
...I'm not drinking the water.
She steps forward, rises on her toes, touches his cheek. Then pulls back fast.
Don't say it. Not today.
I'm keeping count.
She picks up her cloth bag and pushes the door open. The hinge creaks. She's already around the corner.
Lydia comes in, glances at the door hinge, then down at her own shoe tips.
The door's fixed? Who fixed it? You?
Took two of us.
Great. So I'm late. Didn't even get to hand over a nail.
I stopped by the Watch office again.
The clerk said wait. Wouldn't say how long.
The watch... I'm still working on it. Don't rush me.
Not rushing.
Right. You never rush me. That's why I'm worse.
She pushes her bracelet up her wrist and taps the counter three times.
I came here today to talk business.
Just tell me— how much are you?
How much am I what.
You. All of you. I'll buy you. Then you won't get smashed up here every day.
...No. Wait. Why does that sound so bad out loud.
I don't sell people.
Including myself.
I know. I'm not here to— I just talk fast.
Then different. I won't buy you. I'll buy one day of you.
What do you want. Say it straight.
Straight, and I can't say it. Let me go around first.
I'm not buying you. I'm buying one day you're closed. Okay?
There are price tags on the wall. I'm not on them.
Oh, you even reject people by the shelf.
Then something else. Not on the shelf—one day of you.
One day closed. Whatever your shop misses, I'll cover it.
A day doesn't bring in much.
Then I'll go by those days the door was broken, and the day the goods fell over. Two thousand.
Too much.
It's my own money. Not the family's.
It's money for closing. Nothing else.
If you think I'm buying something else, say it now, and I'll take it back.
The shopkeeper looked at her for a moment.
One day.
...Really? Don't laugh.
Not laughing.
Then it's settled.
First thing tomorrow, don't open for business—open the door and wait for me.
The door opened. Lydia was already outside, her hair pinned neat.
I'm early. Didn't wake you, did I?
Awake.
Do I look good? Just say one thing, and I won't ask again.
You look good.
...You said that way too fast.
This shop's mine today.
She stepped in sideways.
The door closed.
The shop door was open. Lydia sat on the stool outside the counter.
I thought about it the whole way. Next time it's my turn to bring food.
Don't say no. I've already decided.
There's something you should know.
All right. Tell me.
Eleanor came by a few days ago. She fixed the door.
She told me how she feels. Before you did.
...Before me.
What did she say— no, don't tell me. Those are her words.
I wasn't going to speak for her.
She stands. The stool scrapes back half a foot. Her hand stays flat on the counter.
I thought I was good at planning things.
Turns out I didn't even know she'd gotten ahead of me.
I'm sorry.
I shouldn't have used money to dance around asking for your day. And I shouldn't have kept it from her.
Keep the money. That's for closing your shop. Nothing to do with this.
I know.
I won't make this a secret.
Starting today, I won't buy your days in private anymore.
She pulls out her hairpin, presses it back in, pushes the door open. This time the hinge doesn't creak.
Lydia pushes the door open, hands empty, the bracelet turning halfway around her wrist.
I said next time it was my turn to bring food.
And then I got to the ration station and didn't buy a single thing.
Never mind. That's not what I came for today.
What did you come for?
Came to say congratulations.
With Eleanor's temper, if she speaks first, she really means it.
Don't mess with her. She's all sharp talk, but one harsh word sticks with her for half a year.
Noted.
Good. Then I'm done.
She pulls a stool over and sits, back to the shopkeeper, turns the bracelet, a drop of water lands on the back of her hand.
Done talking, and you're still sitting.
Legs ache. That staircase down from up top is too long.
You've walked that staircase.
...Yeah. Walked it plenty of times. Today it just aches.
Lydia. Turn around.
Don't look. My makeup's not done. I'm ugly.
You're crying.
I'm not—oh, come on, do you have to say that out loud too?
Fine. I'm crying. Happy?
Why?
Just tell me—a person comes with a friend to see someone, and while she's watching,
she gets caught up in it herself. What do you call that?
That day you stood in front of the thug.
And you put the bracelet in the drawer and told me not to sell it.
And the day the door closed, you didn't ask for anything more.
I like you. That's all there is.
But she said it first. She's my friend. Has been since we were kids.
I don't want to be the one who squeezes in from behind.
So I'm backing out. After today, I won't come anymore.
I like you too.
...What did you say? No—wait, say that—
No. Don't say it again. I can't take it twice.
But I can't decide this alone.
You really want out?
I want out. And I don't. Do you have to make me spell it out?
Spell it out.
...I don't. But I'm afraid it'll hurt her.
I like you too. We talk about this when she's here.
The shopkeeper takes a bag of basic food from the shelf and sets it by her hand.
Eat first. We'll talk about whether you're going after.
You... I'm crying, and you give me this.
I like you too. If we talk, all three of us talk.
Eleanor has to say what she thinks herself.
You want me to go ask her? Be your messenger?
No messages. All three of us, face to face.
Face to face... what if she just leaves after she hears it?
Then she leaves on her own.
That's too harsh.
But somehow that makes me feel a little safer.
I have to tell her about that day myself first. You don't get to bring it up first.
Okay.
Then it's settled. I'm not backing out. For now.
She wipes her face, fixes her hairpin, and pushes the door open. Her steps are slow.
The two come in one after the other. Eleanor carries a cloth tool bag, and Lydia pushes a stool to her feet.
She says she has something to say, and it has to be here.
Hah. Like a goods handover.
There's an account I need to come clean about first.
After you fixed the door, I came here. I paid him to close the shop for a day.
It was my own money. I was here that day.
I didn't know you'd spoken first. But I didn't tell you either. That's my fault.
Eleanor sets the cloth bag on the counter. She stares at the drawstring, silent for a long time.
One day.
You paid him to stay closed for a day. Unbelievable. That's just like you.
Yeah. Yell at me.
I haven't yelled yet. I'm deciding which part to start with.
Hey, you knew about this too?
Knew. She said she wanted to tell you herself.
...Fine. I'll say this much: you two didn't lie to me about that.
You two talk first. I'm listening.
The shopkeeper retreats behind the counter and pushes the basic food bags aside.
You sure know how to dodge.
That's for you two to say.
I want to keep you both. But you two have to talk first.
You said that up front. Saves me from guessing.
Then... I'll say my side first.
The shopkeeper pushes a stool between the two of them and goes back behind the counter.
Sitting closer is supposed to make us talk it out? Ridiculous.
Sit closer. It'll save you energy when you yell at me.
Then I'll talk. I like him. I told him a few days ago.
I was going to leave. Stay out of your way.
If you leave, who's going to pick fabric with me? Who's going to argue prices with me?
Don't give me that. If you leave, I'll have to guess what you're thinking every day.
...Then what do you want? Tell me. I'm listening.
I have three rules.
One, if I'm jealous, I'll say it straight out. Same for you. No keeping it bottled up.
Two, no passing messages. If you have something to say to me, don't go through him.
Three, everyone gets their own time. Don't butt in on my day.
And no more paying for things like that.
Okay. I agree to all three.
Then I've got terms too.
I'm not the tag-along. Don't make me feel like the one who just came along with you.
My day, I'll set it up with him myself. I don't need you handing it to me.
And if you ever regret it, say it to my face. Don't go cold on me.
You sure know how to make demands.
You started it. I'm just following.
...Fine. I'm nodding.
I'm nodding too.
I want to keep both of you.
That only counts if all three of us nod.
I just nodded. How many times do you want me to nod.
She nodded. I nodded. You're the only one left.
I'm nodding.
...Don't laugh. I'm about to cry again.
Cry about what. The door's only been fixed a few days. Don't wipe your snot on the counter.
Eleanor digs a screwdriver out of her cloth bag, crouches, and tightens a screw by the hinge another half turn.
I'll tell you later which day I'm taking.
Then I'll take what's left. No, wait, I want to pick first too.
Then we each pick our own. If they clash, we fight about it face to face.
Fine. We'll fight then.
Opening up today. You two sit down and stay out of the way.
Heh. I'm keeping score.
The hinge swings. No sound.
Good! Rule one: if she isn't in a hurry to leave, whatever you do, don't ask 'What else do you have?' Just say—your hair clip looks nice today.
If she's not wearing a hairpin, compliment something else! The hairpin isn't the point. Look at her, not just the counter.
That's all I've prepared. They all work! Don't laugh. Thank me after you use them.
Fine, I'll stay out of it. ...But if she asks, I'll say you finally said something decent today.
One more thing. She mentions you more than she mentions today's earnings. I assume most of it is complaining.
She can't admit she misses you every time she sees me.
If she knew I came here, she'd kill me. So I'll say it straight: if you really like her, I can give you a hand.
Because she's my friend. And because every time she tells me what you two talked about, it ends up being about prices! I get anxious just listening.
No tests today. I came to say thanks.
After her mother came back, she finally let herself sleep. When I went to see her the day before yesterday, she'd slept until noon.
I used to tell her to go upstairs and ask old connections to fix it. She wouldn't listen, and I got angry with her.
When she was at her worst, I was still telling her which dress would look more spirited. ...I wasn't hearing a word she said.
I told her. She cursed me out, then asked whether I'd eaten. I suppose that means she forgave me.
She said she wants to help you find customers. When she gets enthusiastic, she runs ahead.
Just tell her clearly how far you can go.
That will do for today.
Lydia came by, didn't she? Did she teach you that?
A few lines. But asking you to stay longer was my own idea. You look... well today.
I slept three hours last night.
She really will teach you anything! ...That's more like it.
My mother complains I put everything away too neatly and now she can't find anything. She shooed me out and told me to find something of my own to do.
To sell goods! ...And to sit for a while.
That plaque... she gave you that too? She can praise a shop she likes for ages, but she rarely puts her own name out there.
She said she'd help you bring in customers. If you want to thank her, do it yourself. Don't route everything through me.
I saw an old brooch. The dealer says a famous person wore it, but I just like the petals. Is the extra price worth it?
It's still in the shop. I haven't paid. Don't laugh at me for buying things just because they look good.
Looking good is a reason. If someone famous wore it, make them show proof. If you like the petals, negotiate the price of the petals.
So it's not that I don't appreciate it - I just don't have to pay for the story too?
I thought you'd say this kind of thing is useless.
Eat something proper first. A piece of cake later doesn't count as lunch.
...I came to teach you how to care about her, and you practiced on me first. Fine, I won't pass that part on.
You can bring your own problems to me too.
I'm not asking about her today. I have something of my own I can't decide on.
Back to you. She hates being left to guess. When the time comes to speak, don't wait for her to ask, and don't start by worrying she'll laugh at you.
You're taking this seriously.
I only teach this much. What you say to her, you'll have to come up with yourself. Don't recite my lines—she'll know.
Speaking of the brooch—do you have anything here that goes with it? Show me.
Look first. The price is the price.
I like you. I don't want to be just the shopkeeper you come to when something's wrong. I won't make you guess anymore.
...Did she teach you that too?
She only taught me to say it clearly. Who I like doesn't need her teaching.
...Me too. I like you! Did you hear me?
There's still dust on my hand.
Should I let go?
Who told you to let go?
...I understand.
We'll keep doing business. Don't start avoiding me just because we've had this talk.
Lydia brings you up every time I see her lately. She says I should hear you out instead of shutting you down with prices.
Everyone I see lately asks what I'm going to do next.
Live a good life. Find proper work, look after Mother. ...And sometimes, I want to come here. Don't make me spell out every word!
She really thinks I can't tell. ...Move your cup this way. It's in the way there.
Which baker made this bread? It's not the one I know, so I'm not buying it.
Do it again. He missed it.
Oh! I promised to look at clothes with someone. Take your time—no need to see me out.
Did you not just say that shop was closing early today?
...There is another one! Just enjoy yourselves!
Your shawl! You forgot it again.
Do not spend the whole time talking about stock.
I booked a table for three. She's been too busy to eat lately, so I'm dragging her out. Of course I'm coming too—otherwise you two would stare at each other and who'd start the conversation?
You two didn't spend the whole time talking about goods afterward, did you? I went to trouble to clear the space. I wasn't doing it for your entertainment.
I'd say I helped. Next time she complains about you, I only need to hear half of it.
She even handed me my shawl that day. ...She always remembers things like that.
I bought that brooch last time! He couldn't prove anyone famous wore it, so I negotiated on the piece itself and got a good discount. It goes with two of my dresses. Both look good.
It's not that one word from you made me stop liking it... It's just that now I can like it without worrying about being fleeced.
From now on, I can ask you about my own things too, right? Next time I'll bring my own problems. Don't get annoyed!
...Fine. I'll think my own business through first.
You really know how to kill the mood. Fine, let's look at the stock.
...I'll hold you to that.
By the way, those two dresses still need something to go with them. What have you taken in lately?
Look for yourself. We'll talk price if you find something.
Anyway, this time I'm going up there as someone who doesn't just have everything handled for her.
Lydia found me a trading house that handles household goods and growing equipment. They need someone to organize delivery records and check stock.
I tried it for two days. The first day they only let me count against the list. Then I caught a crate with the wrong model number, and they let me keep the books myself.
They did! My employer is arranging a work pass for me. I'll run between both levels for now, and once I know the place better, I'll find a room upstairs.
Mother stays below, doing the work she has now. Her restrictions are still there. My having a job doesn't mean her case is closed.
The research office asked me to organize handover records. Some of it has to be done upstairs, with a separate work pass.
I want to go. There's still a lot I don't understand, so I'll do what I can first. Lydia asked about a room I can stay in short-term, not far from there.
Then I'll have to look forward to you getting off work. Set the time aside in advance. You make time, and so do I.
...Why have you not asked whether I will still come?
I was about to ask you out.
...I will. I just cannot run down here with a bag of stock every time I think of you.
Lydia even told me to say it slowly, so you wouldn't think I was leaving.
Does she think we're that bad at talking to each other?
...Sometimes she's not wrong.
My mother's official result came through too. She'll decide about the research and where to live herself. I'll focus on doing my job well first.
Mother's review isn't finished. She lives under her current registration. My getting a pass doesn't mean she'll suddenly move upstairs.
I'm borrowing your place to rest my feet! I spent all morning rearranging a jewelry shop's display. My legs are sore.

The first time, I packed all the brightest pieces together. From a distance you couldn't see anything. Then I left some space, and even the plainest piece got questions. The owner wants me to do it again.
Look here. The petals aren't even the same color.
That is much better than praising how I arrange a display.
You do know how to be thoughtful.
...Why are you so good at talking today?
Good—show me what you've taken in lately. My legs are resting; my eyes aren't.
Tell me which one you want, then we'll talk price.
No rush. I meant to go see the new dresses, but halfway there I came around to this place instead.
The dresses will not run away. Today I came to see whether you had learned to give a compliment—and it seems you have.
Next time you see her, don't keep asking whether work's going well. Sometimes she wants you to notice her new hair ornament.
You changed yours too. You taught me to look at the person, not just the counter. It works.
...You—why are you looking so closely? I told you to look at her!
...Thank you.
...I gave her that one! Is your eye for detail good or bad?
Since I'm already at the counter, show me what you've recently taken in. Don't fob me off with just the most expensive piece.
You can look. Whether you buy is up to you.
There are two days next week when I can come down early. I wrote them down.
When things get busy upstairs, everyone says 'this will only take a moment.' If I don't set time aside in advance, my own plans always get pushed back.
Those two days are ours. Remember that.
Has Lydia been by lately?
She came a few days ago. Then she stopped.
She says she's busy. I mentioned that new shop she's been wanting to visit. She didn't even ask where it was. Just said she'd made other plans.
When she really doesn't want to go out, she complains her shoes pinch or her dress doesn't fit. She wouldn't say she's busy without even hearing where.
Does she talk about her own things when she's here?
She does.
...Before, whenever she talked about you, it was all 'he should do this' and 'you should do that.' Lately she doesn't say a word.
I haven't decided what to ask her yet. And don't suddenly pretend you don't know her just because I asked. That would look worse.
The customer business stays as usual. Whatever's already arranged, I'll make clear.
I didn't ask about customers. These past few days you didn't come, I kept looking at the door.
...I know. Hearing you say that makes it even harder to leave.
From now on, if you want to ask her out, just ask her. I've been... busy lately.
We've already talked directly.
Good. Then my job here is done.
It's not like I have to come around here every day. Last time I came this way, I missed a dress I wanted to see.
...I had other plans later.
If you don't want to talk about it, fine. Don't fob me off with something else.
I thought I'd be happy once it worked out. Happy for her, and happy for you.
It's just... when she told me you'd met, the first thing I thought about was what you talked about. She didn't mention me, and then I was angry at myself for caring.
Don't comfort me. When you look at me seriously, I can't finish a sentence.
Let me think on my own. That's enough for today.
...Then tell her. Every time I think of how she will look at me, I lose all my words.
Honestly... now it's my turn to wait for you to say it clearly. Until you do, don't make me wait in secret. I'll go see her myself too.
I'm not saying I was just passing by this time. I like you.
At first, I just wanted things to go better for her.
You remembered my brooch, and you listened to all those little things. I started looking forward to coming here—and then feared you only asked how she was.
But Eleanor doesn't know yet. You have to tell her the truth. What do you actually want? Don't leave us both guessing.
I was afraid a longer one would make you shut me down with prices again.
All right. I'm not asking you to decide today.
...You—don't answer so fast. Hear me out first.
Lydia says she likes me. I like her too. I don't want to lie and say she's just a friend. I had to tell you myself.
...And then? You really dare say it to my face!
Of course I'm angry! ...I've felt something was off for a while. She didn't come, and you didn't mention her. I thought I was imagining things.
Whenever I asked about her, you changed the subject. You knew you should have told me earlier!
So what do you want now? To break up with me?
I want to be with you. And I have fallen for her too. I owe you both truths, to your face.
...You're honest, at least. What about her? What did she say?
She said she'd come find you herself.
She'll find me?

A couple of days ago I was still thinking that if she never came again, maybe I could pretend none of it happened. Then I wanted to go find her myself. To ask what she was hiding... and afraid she'd actually tell me.
At dinner she held up that bread and imitated a customer. I nearly spilled my water laughing. When she came back for her shawl, I wanted to ask her to sit down again.
I have imagined more evenings together like that. I want you, and I want her to stay too. ...Do not think that means I have stopped being jealous.
After you two talk, I'll still be here.
Let me talk to her first. I have questions for her that you can't answer for me.
Don't suddenly stop coming to see me these next few days. Don't think that because I'm angry, you should stay away.
I'll open as usual tomorrow. If you come, you'll see me.
...Hmph.
I went to find her. ...No, she came to find me first.
The moment she walked in she asked, 'Didn't you say if you like someone, don't make them guess?' That's what I taught her! She used it to shut me up.
I said that was about her. She said: 'So it doesn't count when it's your turn?'
I said if she didn't want to see me again, I just wouldn't—before I finished, she cut in: 'See? Answering for me again.'
I used to watch you two refuse to open your mouths and want to say it for you. Now it's my turn, and I don't even know where to start.
Then she asked what I actually wanted. I said I wanted to see you. Not to walk you to the door and stand outside waiting.
She said she wants the three of us to be like that day again, talking until we lose track of time. She won't stop minding all at once, and she won't give me every agreed evening either.
I said we'd make separate plans. When we go shopping together, she has to finish the trip with me. Don't keep thinking about coming back to see you.
Then we both cried. ...She won't admit it. Don't ask her.
She said she'd come with me next time. I've already thought about what to wear, but the words are still fighting in my head.
Then I will say the most important bit first. I want to be with you.
Me too.
Then it'll be your turn next time. Think before you speak. Don't just sit there saying, 'Whatever you want.'
I want this. ...Give me your hand.
I'm willing too. This time don't leave me at the door.
I only came to help out a little.
You certainly helped thoroughly.
Then I'm charging a referral fee. One kiss... not in front of the whole shop.
Can't you slow down?
Well, you can teach me that later.
She told you I cried, didn't she? She cried first.
I was the one who got out a handkerchief first! ...Oh, never mind. We can argue about that later.
I have thought it over. I want to try this, the three of us. And I will tell you when I am jealous. Do not expect sudden generosity.
And when you ask me out, you cannot spend the whole time looking at her.
You've made plans with her too. I know. Don't keep checking the time today and making me feel I'll have to leave first.
Today's time is yours.
...Kiss me again.
...So when it actually happens, I'm not that good with words after all.
I spent a long time in front of the mirror. If you say nothing, I shall have to compliment myself.
I see. You look beautiful today.
...I thought I'd have to remind you.
Finished yet? I spent ages choosing what to wear, and that is all the attention I get?
...How long do you want me to stay today?
I missed you.
Where are we going today? We're already here.

Mm. I picked it for this place. I tried one on first, but it looked too much like meeting a relative. Then I changed to this one and couldn't give up the color of the other. I turned in front of the mirror for ages.
You chose well. You don't need lessons now.
When I was teaching you to compliment her, I never thought one sentence could be so hard to answer. ...Then look a little longer. It's not just for the glance at the door.
Do you remember the display I arranged for the jewelry shop? The owner came to me again. I want to try a different layout this time.
Today is our agreed time. I just want to hear you say it once.
Work's fine. Everyone upstairs knows which day I leave early. I told them I'm coming to see you - no sneaking around.
...Last time it was her turn to keep you company, right? I won't ask how long. I'm a little jealous! Don't laugh. I just want to know.
Don't recite everything you said to her the moment you see me. It makes me feel like I'm here to audit the books.
I only want to say one thing today—when I come back from upstairs, the first person I want to see is still you. Don't think one more person means I'll ask for less.
I wasn't planning to ask you to.
Then hold me tighter.
Don't say 'let's just eat something' today.
If we don't plan it, someone always ends up busy until the food's cold and calls it dinner.
She means you, and herself too.
Now you're finishing my sentences for me?
You used to finish mine more than I do yours.
Then I'll just—
Sit down. You don't have to make room for us today.
I didn't say I was leaving. It's just... last time I sat here, at this point I'd be finding an excuse.
You don't need one this time. Your portion is still here.
...Then I won't go. We haven't had the pastries yet.
This dessert wasn't bought especially for us, was it?
It was at first. Today I wanted some too. I'm usually direct. Only liking you took a little practice.
Let me try yours too. Hers has even more cream than mine.
All that choosing, and you still want someone else's.
You just took something from his bowl!
The plaque is still up. Business, like I said, depends on you.
So are you here to inspect the business today?
Not today. Both the people I wanted to see are here.
Both of you sit closer. I don't want to look at you across the table.
Gladly! Move this way. I saved you some dessert.
Any closer and there will be no room left on my side.
And you have the nerve to say that about me?
Lydia drapes her gauzy shawl over the windowsill and leans in, reaching over to push the ledger in front of you aside.
No more number-crunching! Come on, settle a debate for me—does this one flatter my dress better than yesterday's?
You've asked three times between the street corner and here. My ears are about to grow calluses.
You just gave me some half-hearted answer, so of course I need our sharpest eye as the judge!
Today's suits you better.
And someone's new earrings are pretty eye-catching too.
Ooh, caught you! She spent ages fussing in front of the mirror before we left.
Lydia, keep your mouth shut— ...hey, I just threw them on. Do they look good?
You both look good. Come closer, let me see.
Eleanor's ears go warm, but she follows your lead and leans close to the windowsill beside Lydia.
This is close enough, isn't it... No half-hearted answers. Tell me exactly what looks good.
Come on, praise me! Last night at the banquet, someone was going on again about that old mantel clock they picked up here.
Said it keeps better time than the new one upstairs — I nearly wagged my tail clean off listening.
And you didn't take the chance to brag that you spotted it first?
Oh! I was too busy being happy for you — clean forgot to steal the credit!
Then stay a while longer. Call it celebrating on my behalf.
Lydia leans over the windowsill with a grin and tips her sequined earlobe toward you.
Then look at this first — new ear cuffs, picked them out specially this morning. Pretty, aren't they?
Well, since you've had your look, bring out your latest haul and let me see too.
Just a pair of ear cuffs is so plain — I need one more piece to really make a show of it.
Pick whatever you like. The bill still stands, though.
Stingy! Fine, charge me — I'm not leaving till I dig out the piece that suits them best.
Lydia asked me to pass along a message—she got held up with some errands today, so she'll be a bit late.
Eleanor props her elbow on the windowsill, then suddenly leans in close to the window, the corners of her eyes curving with a smug little arc.
But until she gets here, this whole stretch of free time belongs to me alone.
That last part I added myself—no crossing it out, and put that ledger down while you're at it.
Taking advantage of me while she's away? Sneaky.
Taking advantage? Please. This is first come, first served.
The tips of her ears warm slightly, yet her fingers hook over the edge of the window frame with perfect self-assurance, not retreating even a little.
Anyway, I got here first, so for the next half hour you can only look at me—and keep your attention on our conversation.
Lydia leans on the windowsill, chin in her hand, and taps the counter lightly with a fingertip, smiling.
Tomorrow Eleanor and I are heading out for a half-day of shopping. Don't get so busy you forget to eat on time again.
And who was it that stood sighing outside the fitting rooms last time, complaining we took forever picking out one dress?
So we've decided—tomorrow we're simply not bringing you along. Spare someone the grumbling.
Then bring me back a pastry.
Ooh, yes! That new cream pastry shop on the corner—I'll save you the biggest box, promise!
Eleanor reaches over and smooths a crease from your cuff, ears faintly pink as she leans half a step closer.
Two pastries and you're satisfied? ...If there's anything else you want, say it now—I'll pick it up on the way.
Someone was hovering around my nameplate by the alley entrance just now.
Didn't even glance at the goods in the case — came right up and asked if I was really me.
Oh? And how did our big attraction handle that?
I gave him a gracious nod and steered his eyes right back to the vintage shelves.
Coming into a shop and not picking anything out, just staring at the owner — what kind of behavior is that?
You're really getting the hang of this business.
Lydia drapes herself over the windowsill and deliberately tilts her right ear — the one with the rhinestone clip — toward you.
Of course. I've been putting in plenty of work at this window today.
But you — I've been wearing this clip this whole time, and you just enjoyed the show without a single compliment.
Go on, praise her. She's been flipping her hair on that side so long her neck's about to cramp.
It suits you. Noticed it the moment I looked.
You really ought to hear what Lydia's been going on about up there lately.
She gets more worked up over the old trinkets in your shop than over her new dresses.
Oh, come on—that's only because people kept asking about the bracelet on my wrist!
Is that so? And when nobody asks, who brings it up three times unprompted?
Lydia's ears go pink. She bumps Eleanor's shoulder lightly, then turns to look at you through the window.
You're one to talk! Every time you come down claiming it's for business, you lean on that window and don't budge.
I come by to check the merchandise. That's all.
It's quiet today. No rush on anything.
Their eyes meet by the window. Eleanor rests her fingertips on the counter's edge, her expression softening.
Mm. Everything else is long since handled. The rest of today was always meant for you.
Then it's settled—we're camped out here all afternoon, and nobody's allowed to shoo us off.
A new old ornament has taken up residence on the windowsill — gold lacquer with a big red flower slapped on.
Ohh, gold paint and a giant red flower? That's way too loud. I can't even pretend to call it pretty.
Running a shop isn't hosting a tea party. Stuck in the middle of the goods, it grabs the eye — might just sell.
Even so, you can't put it dead center! It looks like some nouveau riche's living room!
Your call. Last time you arranged the display, customers complimented it.
Of course they did! Now nudge it half an inch left — catch a little side light — yes, right there.
She leaned over the windowsill calling out directions, and Eleanor obligingly straightened the base for her.
...I'll admit it. Clearing half the space and letting the light hit it — it does look better than jammed in with everything else.
Hmph. Tacky's fine — but our shop's presentation must never be tacky.
The window frame rattles twice. Before Lydia can finish knocking, Eleanor catches her hand.
Knocking that loud this early? The whole alley can hear you.
I was just worried he was still sleeping in.
Enough talk. Sort this basket of old clothes by thickness first.
Look at her. She snaps at everyone like that.
Used to it.
(Takes out a soft cloth) Oh, that old brass watch is still on the counter today.
I've got a mirror cloth in my bag. Want me to polish the lid for you?
Don't touch it.
Someone from the mine pawned that.
The dust in the seams came up from the shaft.
He said if the dust is gone, it isn't his watch anymore.
Then I'll pay to redeem it, and you can have someone return it to him. How's that?
No need for my name. Just sign it "a friend."
You don't know his name or what floor he lives on, but you've already picked a signature?
Save it. Nobody down here needs your offhand charity.
Let's get to work.
Hey, why'd you stop halfway through?
Okay, okay. I'll finish sorting this basket first. Happy?
You ask.
The man who pawned the watch... did he ever come back for it?
He never meant to.
The shaft shut down. The watch got him through to reopening.
And after it reopened? He saved enough and still didn't redeem it?
Came once a month. Just stood at the window and looked.
Asked if the dust was still on it. If yes, he left.
How have I never heard you mention this?
Has he come by these past two months?
Not since last winter.
So you just keep the watch here?
The ticket hasn't expired. It's still his.
...I made it out to be too simple.
If you know it, roll up your sleeves. This basket's untouched.
Lydia rolls up her cuffs, baring the bracelet on her wrist, and takes the basket of old goods.
Don't worry, I'll sort this whole basket out properly today.
You should've seen it—Eleanor grabbed the bill at dinner; she was so fast I almost couldn't stop her!
If I hadn't stopped you, you'd have left the tip under the plate.
Two people eating ration meals and you pay for three—scared people won't know you're from up above?
Oh, I was just doing it without thinking... Besides, I corrected myself in time!
Oh, right—it just hit me this afternoon, I still have something to do on the other side.
You two take your time. I'll get out of your way.
Stop. What 'other side' is there in the Lower Level? You can't even read all the signs.
Lydia's eyes darted sideways and suddenly fixed on an empty blood bag at the corner of the counter, tied with fine string.
...Huh? Why is this old blood bag pawned here too?
Why are there all these neat little scratches along the seal?
A mother pawned it here.
One blood sale behind the ration station, one mark.
Why keep count?
Afraid of fainting in the queue alley from giving too often.
When this side is full, she'll have enough for the child's medicine.
Lydia bent down and counted the row of faint marks from beginning to end along the window ledge.
One, two, three... That's not right. There are still three empty spots here.
Why did she pawn it to you before filling the row?
Leave it for now. Go do your business.
What kind of person are you! Half a story and then nothing—how am I supposed to walk away!
I don't care. I'm not leaving until I've finished sorting this basket of old goods.
The child recovered. It's not needed anymore.
At home, she can't resist taking it out at night to count.
With it pawned here, she can sleep easy.
She came by last week to buy daily supplies.
...You scared me. I thought something bad had happened.
Then I won't leave this afternoon. I'll stay and help you finish sorting the rest of the goods.
So you don't need to take care of that 'other side' business?
Oh, you knew all along I was making it up, and you still had to call me out!
Roll up your cuffs first, so you don't get dust all over yourself again.
Before closing, a dusty chunk of ore sits at the corner of the counter, leaving a faint gray mark on the wood.
That stone looks heavy. Can I touch it?
A miner's daughter left it.
First piece her dad dug up in the shaft.
Quality's that rough? It wouldn't fetch much in a shop, would it?
Wouldn't. But it's a keepsake.
She's going to work on the Upper Level. Couldn't take it.
Couldn't throw it out either.
She went up there to work. Will those people treat her like she matters?
Hard to say.
Don't touch. It's someone else's.
Okay, I'm just looking closer. I won't mess with someone else's things.
Go ahead. It's dusty.
Wow, it doesn't look big, but it's way heavier in my hand than I thought.
Your fingertips are all black. Wipe them with a handkerchief.
Not yet. A little dust doesn't hurt anything.
(Chewing) ...This taste is brutal. You actually ate this for weeks straight?
More than weeks. Money was tight, so this was all I could buy.
I can get it down. I'm finishing every last bite today.
Wait, you charged me a good bit less than Eleanor said.
Closing price.
Don't fob me off with "closing." Next time I'm picking the expensive stuff.
Even a cheap fruit can't shut you up. Hurry, finish chewing and let's go.
Huh, why is this fruit a little pricier than Eleanor said?
You came shopping dressed that nicely. Who else would he fleece?
Fine. Next time I'll come to the window in old clothes.
Why'd you close up the counter? You won't even sell me a fruit this cheap?
He's locking up for the night. If you want to try it, come back tomorrow.
Then I'll come first thing tomorrow and pick one out myself.
Oh, right. What was the cheap food Eleanor ate every day when she first came?
Why ask that? You'd never get that dry fruit down.
If you could eat it, why couldn't I?
Give me the cheapest one. I'll eat it right here at the window.
Suit yourself. Just don't come begging me for water when it's so bitter you're scowling.
A man with a rough, scarred hand pressed on the windowsill and a chunk missing from his left ear blocked the window.
I'm looking for information on someone.
Those two Upper District women who keep coming around—what time do they usually show, and which route do they take?
We only do business here. I don't ask about customers' backgrounds.
Don't brush me off with shop talk. Especially the one with the bracelet on her wrist—I've had my eye on her for two days.
That bracelet last month that almost changed hands—she redeemed it herself, didn't she?
The one who meant to buy it is still stewing. Since he can't get the bracelet, he wants her to come over for a visit.
Upper Level families have money to burn. Detaining a person is easier to price than a dead object.
If you're not buying, get away from the window.
Stubborn, huh? What kind of junk are you displaying in this shabby window?
He grabs the ore from the counter corner, flecked with ore dust, and tosses it up and down in his palm.
Customer's collateral. Put it down.
A woman with a bracelet? Never seen her.
Playing dumb? Plenty of eyes on the street saw them duck into your window.
If you keep your mouth sealed, don't blame us when we wreck this stall.
Who wanted to buy the bracelet last month?
You're not worthy of asking that person's name. Just watch your mouth.
Be smart: give us those two women's whereabouts, and you'll save yourself some pain.
Put it down and get out. Now.
The ore slams back onto the counter corner with a dull thud and stops right beside the old copper pocket watch.
Fine. It's down.
But your window glass looks thin, and that beat-up copper pocket watch at the edge could easily fall.
Risk your whole shop for two outsiders—ask yourself if it's worth it.
Everyone at the window is a customer. If the glass breaks, I'll replace it myself.
Got nerve. We'll see about that.
He raps his knuckles hard twice on the iron window frame, then turns and melts into the alley shadows.
No line at the ration station today, of all things. Saved us a lot of time getting here.
Forget that. Look, something's off with the shopkeeper.
What's wrong? Did something happen at the shop?
Someone came looking for you at noon.
For me? I barely know anyone in the Lower Level.
Asked what time you come by, which route you take.
Specifically mentioned the bracelet on your wrist.
The one who didn't get the bracelet at the black market last month?
They haven't let it go.
Said your family's rich. Willing to pay ransom.
Absurd. That lowlife is plotting to kidnap someone and extort her family!
And to them, I count as someone from up top too. They'll definitely come for us both.
(Reaches to slip off the bracelet) If it's what they're after, just give it to them.
Keep it on.
They want the person, not the bracelet.
Then let's report it to the security bureau right now. We can't just sit and wait.
The Lower Level security bureau won't even lift a pen unless there's blood.
Then I'll give them my family name and make them sit up and deal with it!
That'd work. With a big Upper Level name bearing down, they won't dare brush it off.
What did the man from noon look like?
Missing a piece of his left ear. Scar on the back of his hand.
Picked up the ore on the counter corner, then put it back.
Eleanor, maybe you should stay away from here for a few days.
Spare me. Do you really think I'm the type to go hide?
Of course you're not. Then we stick together, every step of the way.
Leave before dark.
Take the busy road past the ration station.
We'll be fine on the main road together, but what about you, alone in the shop?
I've always run the shop alone.
You're so stubborn. Lock the shutters early tonight.
Lydia pulls down her cuff, completely covering the bracelet on her wrist.
First thing tomorrow we'll file a report with the Security Bureau, then come straight here to tell you.
See you tomorrow. Don't you dare hide anything from us.
Be careful out there.
The Security Bureau was useless. Even after I gave my family name, they just scribbled two lines in a logbook.
I've stuffed this pile of old clothes at the bottom. Let's just lock up early today.
Wait, why did three people just turn into the alley?
The one in the middle—half his left ear really is missing!
Head for the ration station.
No, the crossing by the ration station is blocked too!
They're coming at the window with iron bars. Get back!
Fall back to the back alley.
There are footsteps in the back alley too. We can't fall back!
Then stay by the windowsill and don't run, or they'll drag you into the dark!
Hold steady by the windowsill.
(Grabs your sleeve through the window) Don't try to stop them, they're armed!
An iron bar slams into the shutter's edge, and several panes in front of the window shatter.
Stay back! I'm not even wearing that bracelet today!
Take the goods. Leave the people.
He's grabbing Lydia by the collar!
I've got that half bottle of perfume from the counter—take this!
And this wrench—let go of her!
Shout toward the alley mouth.
Security Bureau patrol's at the ration station corner—over here!
He's clutching his eyes and cursing—the other two are hauling him off!
They're gone... Actually, I made up the Security Bureau part.
Only you'd think of that. My legs went weak... Wait, why is your sleeve covered in blood?
Just a scratch.
A scratch? Blood's dripping down your wrist! Sit down!
(Grabs the old clothes on the counter, hands shaking) Let me bind it—why won't this tear when I'm in a hurry...
Forget the old clothes, just rip the gray one!
Hey, put your left arm up here at the window.
Look how crooked that bandage is—you wrapped it one-handed. It's bleeding through again and you didn't even notice?
It's stopped.
Don't talk tough! Hold still—I'll clean the dried blood off the edges with soapy water.
Then I'm wrapping it tight with a clean strip.
Last night, when those three were smashing the window with clubs—you had to stand in front and take it?
Pull a stunt like that again, and I won't wait for anyone else—I'll knock some sense into you with a wrench myself.
Listen! Three days, no heavy loads. I'll come by tomorrow and the day after to move things for you.
And me! I brought a broom specially to sweep up the broken glass.
Guess what I did at the Public Order Department last night?
I slammed the duty officer's desk!
Once I gave our family name, I stood there until he'd filled a whole page of the case file.
By the way, the three broken window panes go on my tab.
And that half bottle of perfume in the corner—I sprayed it all over those bastards' faces last night. I'll pay you for it.
Forget the glass. Just sweep the floor clean.
Then it's settled! You won't find a single shard left when I'm done.
Hey, wait... what's this old brass pocket watch doing under the broken glass?
The lid's been knocked clean off.
You made a point of telling me—not one speck of the ore dust inside is to be wiped off. I remember.
Here, I caught it all on paper and poured it back into the watch case. Quick, put it in the drawer.
Thanks. Last night scared you, didn't it?
Of course it did. When I got grabbed by the collar yesterday, I was terrified.
My legs wouldn't stop shaking. Back home last night, I couldn't even hold a cup steady.
But before I left today, I put this bracelet right on my wrist for all to see!
This is a place I care about. No one's scaring me off, and I won't hide it.
...You've got some backbone after all. But once you've swept outside, go back to the Upper Level.
No need for two people to keep watch at the window.
That won't do! You handle your heavy goods, I'll sweep my floor. I'll be back tomorrow and the day after just the same!
Stick out your left arm—let me see if that cloth strip is bleeding through.
Lydia got called home for dinner today—she couldn't get out of it.
The wound's scabbed over. I can move the boxes.
Stop acting tough. I'm counting this box of rations under the window today.
Eleanor bends down, lifts the cardboard box, and hands packet after packet of rations up to the counter.
This packet's seal is split; it won't fetch a good price. Keep it for yourself.
Those two gray-stained old clothes underneath are still sturdy. I pressed them down at the bottom of the box for you.
Take a break. Don't wear yourself out.
Moving a few packs of food isn't tiring. Not like you blocking those thugs with your arm.
If you hadn't stepped in, Lydia would've been dragged off, and your hand would've been ruined.
You don't even frown when the dressing is changed, but you insist it doesn't hurt.
She braces both hands on the windowsill, fingertips digging into the wood, and lowers her voice.
I've been thinking about that day these past two days, and the more I think, the angrier I get.
You're supposed to be a penny-pinching pawnshop owner. How can you be so stupid when it counts?
...Forget it. I wasn't planning to keep it bottled up forever anyway.
I like you.
Eleanor.
Why call me so seriously all of a sudden? My ears are burning.
You gently set the rations you just took back on the counter and look up at her outside the window.
What are you staring at? Every word I said was clear enough.
Stop spacing out. Did you hear me?
Eleanor gripped the window frame and lunged forward, stealing a quick kiss on your cheek through the window.
Don't laugh—put today's crate away first!
Give me your left arm. The strip you tied one-handed came loose again.
She bends through the window and rewraps your loose bandage tight.
New clothes today.
Oh? I thought you only had eyes for stock and the ledger.
Dinner at home was so stifling. I went back to change before coming down.
Oh, and Security got back to me this morning.
Those three haven't dared show up at the ration station for days.
(Takes a deep breath) But I actually came today on serious business.
I want to buy you. All of you.
...Don't laugh yet.
Explain.
Oh, with you looking at me like that, I forgot where to even start.
Sit first.
The second I touched the stool I got nervous. I'll stand and say it.
I'm not for sale.
Fine, fine. Then could you close up for a day tomorrow?
I'll pay two thousand credits to cover tomorrow's lost business.
Where'd the money come from?
My own saved-up allowance. I didn't touch the family accounts.
Is two thousand enough for a day's earnings? If not—
No, wait, that's all I saved. Two thousand it is.
I practiced that line all the way from the elevator. Nearly took the wrong alley.
Tomorrow. Opening time.
It's a deal, then! I'll be waiting at the window tomorrow morning!
Why are you only raising the shutter now?
I've been standing at the window forever. The ration station line has looked me over several times.
No business today.
Of course I remember. I came first to claim the window in case you backed out.
(Steps back half a pace, hands behind her back) So... nothing to say?
Same clothes as yesterday, but I swapped hairpins three times at the mirror this morning.
I finally settled on this one. Quick, tell me if it suits me.
You look at her and nod slightly.
A nod doesn't count. I want to hear you say it.
People are watching.
Let them watch. I'm only asking if you think it looks nice.
It does look nice.
...Oh my, you answered so readily I don't know what to say next.
Last night I almost booked us a table in advance, but I held back.
Where do you want to go?
Today's all yours to decide. I'd happily spend the whole day right here watching the pocket watch with you.
Let's walk and see.
Okay, boss.
The window shutter slowly rolled down.
I couldn't sleep properly last night, so I just sat up and put all my hairpins away in their box.
Um... has Eleanor come by these past couple of days?
I just knocked on her door, and her roommate said through the crack that she wasn't in.
But no matter how angry she gets, she's never hidden from me with an excuse like that.
Boss, have I been too noisy lately? Did I get on her nerves?
Sit down first.
You telling me to sit so seriously makes me even more nervous.
Before you came that day, did you think about her?
I wasn't planning to keep it from her forever. I just wanted that one day from you first... Why ask that all of a sudden?
The day before you came to make your offer, she came by.
She said she liked me, kissed me, and left.
Her fingertips jerked back from the counter's edge, and she gripped the bracelet on her wrist.
The day before... So she beat me to it.
Then... how did you answer her?
That's between her and me.
Why didn't you tell me yesterday? And there I was, pestering you to say my hairpins looked nice...
...I'm sorry, boss.
But you're not refunding those two thousand credits. You really did close up for a whole day yesterday.
Still going to find her?
(Takes a breath) Of course. I'll talk it out with her face to face.
...I just hope her roommate's the one who opens the door.
(She props herself on the sill; her expression is hard to read.) Boss, good news.
I went to see Eleanor.
I told her about what happened outside that day.
(She lifts her chin in an imitation of Eleanor.) She just said, dry as could be, 'I know. Go on.'
Then she told me she had kissed you. I did not know what else to say. I just felt I should quietly disappear.
You two… I'm glad. Well, I'll be off.
(She has just turned away, then turns back to the window.) ...
Lydia.
Her shoulders tremble.
Ugh, so embarrassing. (She wipes her face hastily with the back of her hand.)
I like you.
That day the three of us squeezed in here and shared that pack of instant noodles. When I got home, I buried myself in the blanket and giggled like an idiot.
But she... told you first.
I'll bow out.
Do you really want to give up?
I... want to. Stop asking. I want to. I am willing.
Stop asking... If you keep asking, I will not be able to lie to myself anymore.
(Hands her a tissue.) All right, wipe your tears. If anyone sees, they will think I did something to you.
(She wipes her tears and laughs.) You... you really did bully me.
I like you too.
...What did you say? I think I misheard.
I like you too.
Then what about Eleanor? You cannot mean to have both of us—
Is that not allowed?
Oh, come on~ Since when were you this shameless?
Fine. I cannot help liking you. I will find a chance to talk to Eleanor.
Lydia! Stop pulling. I can walk by myself!
(She lets go of Eleanor's wrist.) Who was it, two streets back, making excuses and dragging her feet? I know. I am just not saying.
(She pretends to be calm and straightens her rumpled cuff.) Lydia tells me you bullied her.
When I asked more, she would not say. She insisted I come and hear it from you face to face.
You'll hear it for yourself in a minute.
(She pulls out the chair with practiced ease and sits back against the sill.) Now I am here. Talk. I want to see what the two of you are scheming.
♥Mmph♥(Eleanor's lips taste of an energy bar)
(Pokes her head in.) The line behind us is still backed up.
Why do you always pick a time like this... (Her ears turn red; she covers her face with her hand.)
♥Mmm♥ (A faint floral scent lingers on her lips.)
(Her eyes widen)
Eleanor is still watching...
I like both of you, so... I want you both.
So that is what you meant by bullying! Hmph, your hide is thick enough for a bulletproof vest!
