Is the locket still around your neck?
It's there. When I was two short earlier, I took it out for a look, then put it back.
A clean cloth is pushed to her hand. She picks it up and wipes the dust from between her fingers.
The dirt on my hands isn't bothering anyone... but thanks.
Tomorrow I'll see that detective myself. Don't come. If he sees a crowd, he'll jack up the price.
I didn't give him all the originals. I kept copies, and noted the time of every meeting.
Thank you. I'm going to find out who did this to my mother.
...Today I was going to say I finally don't have to keep running to your shop.
I didn't say I'd stop coming. Until it's cleared up, I still have to eat.
I can pay. But from now on, you listen to me.
Put the business terms in writing. Whether I take the loan is my decision.
Not just business.
Then no loan.
My mother didn't teach me to pay a debt with myself. That's not how it works down here either.
The money's done. I sold the rest of the goods to another buyer and took an advance on some short work.
Their price wasn't good. I'll have to work a few more days. But I'll manage.
I'll manage. I said I'd find my own way.
The last part of the shortfall, I was planning to cover with the locket.
It's been hanging on me doing nothing. Now I want it to help me find my mother.
I have. Price it like anything else.
No one's following us at either end of the alley, right?
She pulls a thin data drive from her coat's inner pocket and sets it on the counter.
The detective dug it out of my mother's sealed old lab.
Not in a drawer. Stuffed under the lamp stand. Mother always said drawers were for other people to search.
It was locked, and I worked at it all night.
I tried her staff number, the farm code, even old files my father left. None opened it.
Near dawn, I entered my own birthday on a whim.
And it just opened.
Something that dangerous, and the password was my birthday.
What's stored on it?
Half is shifts and ledgers. I haven't had time to look closely.
The most important part is the Nutrifruit research records.
The fruit from the ration station is all seedless. If the Lower Level wants to grow it, they can only wait for the Upper Level to allocate seeds.
Mother ran three full rounds of retests and got Nutrifruit to bear live seeds that could sprout again!
Once this gets out, the Lower Level will never have to hold out its hand every month waiting for the Upper Level to allocate seeds.
At the back are letters from Pastel Company, each more polite than the last, all urging her to stop.
In the end, Mother replied with just two lines: she wouldn't stop.
Less than two weeks later, a charge of embezzling public funds appeared out of nowhere in the farm's ledger.
The detective took the 800 credits, found it too hot to handle, and backed out on the spot.
Now, besides him, only you and I know this drive still exists.
The lock on my door is broken. My roommate has people in and out. I'm even more afraid of losing it at the dump.
Is there anything else on the drive?
There's also a list of farm workers' names, plus a few unpaid old debts.
Under the counter. Locked.
I didn't ask you to hide it for me.
Her fingers press on the data drive for a moment before she slowly pushes it through the window.
Just keep it for a few days. I'll come get it when I've figured out how to use it.
Won't look. Won't touch.
Don't rummage through it while I'm gone... thanks.
She steps back two paces and glances at the lock under the counter.
A dark figure blocks the service window and slams a thick hand on the counter.
Boss, open for business?
Buying or selling?
Neither. I'm here to ask about someone.
That Upper Level girl who's been coming here to sell scrap lately. You know her, right?
Everyone who comes here is a customer.
Don't play dumb. Her mother's still locked up.
The girl swiped a data drive from her mother's lab.
Haven't heard that.
Once the archive room door opened, someone was bound to see.
That girl is guarded and won't talk to strangers, but she comes to this shabby window every day.
He pulls a stack of credits from his coat and slaps it onto the counter.
Three hundred credits. For your trouble.
Pass a message to her for me: hand over the drive, and the higher-ups will drop the case and release her immediately.
If she doesn't... prison gets very cold.
If someone suddenly falls ill in there, no one would find it strange, right?
Take your credits and get out.
Fine. Got backbone. If you don't pass it along, I'll go wait for her downstairs myself.
She gets three days at most. No waiting after that.
Take the credits back. I'll deliver the message.
He snorts, then slowly tucks the stack of credits back into his coat.
Turning down money? Suit yourself—I'm not the one missing out on three hundred.
Then it's settled. In three days, I'll come back to this window for the drive.
The same day I get it, her mother will hear.
What if you go back on your word?
We're only after that drive. No reason to make trouble for a prisoner.
Also, don't get any ideas about going to the Security Department.
That place is a lot busier than you think now. You'd just be walking into a trap.
That girl's got a temper, boss. When you talk her around, you'd better keep your tone soft.
Eleanor walks up to the window empty-handed, her gaze going first to the lock beneath the counter.
Still here?
A runner from the black market came by.
They want you to hand over the data drive in exchange for your mother's release.
So they've set their sights on this place after all.
He shoved three hundred credits at me. I didn't take it.
He also said the cells are cold—no one would find it strange if someone fell ill.
They gave three days. Today is the second.
Three hundred credits? They're buying my mother's life for three hundred credits?!
If I hand over the drive, Mother might come out safe.
But half her life's work would rot in Pastel's drawer, and no one would ever know.
If I just post the files and let the whole Lower Level know about the live seeds...
Mother is still in their hands. She'd become the last card they can crush.
If you were me, what would you do?
Hand over the drive first. I can't gamble with my mother's life.
Sophia's case is dismissed; she is released and barred from returning to the Upper Level.
The research has been handed back. When Mother asks, I'll tell her myself.
First file the bail form with the Security Department, then make the research public.
But it was the Security Department that locked my mother up in the first place!
Bring her out into the open.
Her detention went through a false ledger; the bail goes on a different form.
...True. Last time the Security Department did let me go in the end.
Once the bail form is filed, someone has to sign and take responsibility.
The detective's written note also proves the drive was taken from under the light fixture and never tampered with.
I'll go make a copy. Get the data into the public archive before we hand over the original drive.
She takes the data drive you hold out and grips it in her palm.
If that runner comes again, tell them I'm not handing it over.
And... you didn't take the three hundred credits. I heard just now.
Can't wait any longer. I'll post all the files today!
Detainee Sophia died in custody; cause under investigation.
The files are out, and she's gone... Don't say anything. I'll stand here a moment, then leave.
Detainee Sophia's bail application has been accepted; the case is pending trial; visitation will be announced separately.
Lower Level notice board: research on Nutrifruit seed production at the hydroponic farm has been placed in the public archive.
I sat outside the Security Department all day.
The officer who signed off read the letter, and his face changed on the spot.
They still won't let me see her, but at least on paper, she's safe now.
I've taken care of the public archive too.
What do you want to buy?
You really are direct.
I'll just rest my hand on the windowsill a moment. Standing is fine.
Sit on that low stool.
At your words, Eleanor sits on the low stool outside the window, her shoulders loosening.
When I came back just now, there was a long line at the ration station.
An older woman stopped me and asked if she'd never have to eat Nutrifruit every day again.
I told her there'd only be more Nutrifruit from now on. Her face fell.
If Mother saw the copy I made, she'd definitely nitpick that my handwriting was crooked.
I really don't want to touch Nutrifruit again today.
Just give me something cheap to eat. Sweet is fine. Just for today.
It's been half a month, and I finally got something sweet.
Tomorrow I'll go back to the junkyard to look for goods.
You undercharged me again. I'm not so broke I can't afford this much food.
Forget it. Bring better goods next time to make up for it.
You saw I had to buy today, so you're targeting me, huh?
Hand it over. I can afford this much.
You don't have it here either...? Forget it. I'll go back to eating Nutrifruit.
When there's word from the trial, I'll come tell you.
The application's in. Still waiting for an answer.
You didn't tell me 'it's already fine.'
That's better, actually. People used to say 'don't worry' every time, and then I never saw them again.
I'm taking another short shift tonight. Waiting for news doesn't stop me eating.
I told my roommate that if anyone asks where my mother lives, not to say a word.
My roommate says I'm learning this late.
Your part is in the application too.
I checked your shop address twice.
Afraid that if something happens, I wouldn't be able to find you.
You're here. That's why I dared to take it this far.

The safety review for the person concerned has been accepted. Transfer to temporary protective custody approved; family may visit after verification. This measure does not mean the original case is dismissed.
I... I can see her?
All right. I'll go now. Verify first, then see her.
If it's real, I'll come back and tell you. In person.
Verify the person and the paperwork first. Don't just take a messenger's word that it's done.
I want my mother to confirm it herself. Someone else reading a line for her doesn't count.
No copy. If I'm trading it for her, I can't use her life as collateral and gamble that they won't find out.
I've thought it through. Whether there's another way later is a later problem.
Today, I just want to see her.
Still no confirmation that she can be released, right?
No. Keep applying, or switch to handing over the drive for her release.
I don't want to treat 'processing' as if she's already safe. Get her out first.
Hey! My mother is free!
I saw her myself! The first thing she asked was whether I'd been skipping meals again.
She was exiled to the lower levels. She can't go back to her old farm.
But we're together again. Tonight, I know where she's sleeping.
I saw Mother! She's been moved out, someone's watching over her, and the visit is registered.
She knows what comes next. The research, the threats, going public. I told her everything.
She said to let the protection staff confirm the arrangements first, then send the material out.
She said I'm reckless enough for both of us. Someone in the family has to ask more questions.
I had so much prepared: how she ate in there, why she didn't tell me sooner, whether anyone hurt her.
Not a single one. I just called her 'Mom'.
She said she heard me, and I didn't have to shout.
Now I can ask her slowly.
I used to think that as long as I could get back upstairs, everything would return to the way it was.
But today, when I saw her, I didn't even think about the house up there.
First I'll find a place to live down here. My roommate will help look, and I can keep working.
If I need anything, I'll buy it. At full price. You've done too much for us. I can't have you paying for everything from now on.
But today, I want to thank you properly, once.
All I could say then was that I wanted to save her. You helped me bring her home.

The research on restoring nutrifruit seeds has been handed to independent researchers for verification. The representative of Pastel's station office is suspected of coercion and interference in the case and is now under investigation.
The person concerned is currently under registered protection. The original embezzlement case is still under review; the investigation result does not constitute a final ruling.

The registered protection arrangements have been confirmed. The family is permitted to register a residence in the lower levels and live together, and may carry on normal daily activities. Contact person and address are on file; contact must be maintained during the review of the original case.
Hello. Eleanor says the shopkeeper here tells you the flaws first.
She also says you're not much of a talker, but you're a good person.
I came to see the place she often mentions. And to buy some daily supplies and bring back some food.
She went to work. Before she left, she told me not to wander off and not to buy everything just because it's cheap.
Used to be me giving her that advice; back then she always pretended not to hear.
Thanks for looking after her lately.
She's told me quite a bit about you.
More than she's told me about herself.
I handed the research back, and it doesn't sit well with me.
But don't let her think bringing me back is something she has to apologize to me for.
The material has been sent out. I'll keep cooperating with the review. The rest will take time, step by step.
You were right to get me transferred before publishing. The people with the least protection shouldn't always be the ones paying the price.
That's all. Don't refuse to take my money just because it's me.
She won't take things for free. That part is certainly like me.
When she talks about this place lately, it's not just about what she bought.
And whatever else she said, go ask her yourself. I won't finish her sentences.
A woman in a gray coat stops outside the window, a caregiver registration badge pinned to her chest.
The third window east of the ration station... The map Eleanor drew is more detailed than my shift schedule.
Hello, I'm Sophia. She sent me to buy some daily supplies and said you'd point out the flaws first.
The caps on the top two bottles on the left don't screw tight.
She tests the cap you put on the windowsill through the window and nods, satisfied.
It really is. Then get me some Nutrifruit too.
Wholesale from the ration station? The skin's dull; they're probably empty inside.
She picks up those two bottles, twists the caps, puts them back, and chooses from the row behind.
The data is public now, but no one has handed out live seedlings yet.
You're not going to keep an eye on the farm?
She picks up a Nutrifruit, presses the skin with her fingertip, and holds it under the lamp to look.
My review isn't finished; I have to stay at my registered address, and the guards check on me twice a day.
This morning a worker sent word asking if I'm on the schedule next week, and I couldn't even reply.
The research became everyone's, and I'm left with nothing.
Don't ever tell Eleanor that, or she'll think it's because she made the files public.
By the way, how did she save up those eight hundred credits for the detective?
Scavenged and sold old goods, saved bit by bit.
Really...? Back when she shopped on the Upper Level, she never even glanced at the credits.
She gathered her chosen items by the window and took credits from her coat pocket.
Cut hands, worn clothes. She never said a word about any of it to me at home.
I've picked out daily goods and fruit. Charge me the usual price.
I'll get you ones with tight lids.
That's everything. It's all on the windowsill.
Don't undercharge me just because I'm wearing this gray caregiver's coat.
She's been sleeping deeply these past two days. Last night she was haggling in her sleep.
If she wants to come, she'll come herself. I'm just here to buy things.
She tucked the Nutrifruit into her gray coat pocket, nodded to you, and turned from the window.
Did my mother come by?
She did. Bought some things, paid for them. She told me to ask you.
I knew it.
Then don't ask today!
I brought some goods. This time I'm really here to sell.
My mother gets up earlier than I do now. Two days ago I woke up and found her sitting there repairing an old tray.
She says if her hands aren't doing something, she starts thinking about what happened in there.
I handed her the tools and sat with her for a while.
Nothing special. I just sat there for a while.
I always thought that once she was out, I'd know what to do next.
Work continues, the room needs tidying, meals have to be made. I know all that.
It's just... I don't need to invent a reason to come here so I can ask you for help.
You said that. Remember it.
...You've gotten rather direct lately. Fine, I'll remember that.
You're making this easy for me. All right, I'll get my life steady first.
I'll still come to sell goods. You don't have to ask me what happened every time.
I'm a regular. Ordinary customers don't know what you buy.
The next afternoon, two people come to the window, one behind the other. The first carries half a sack of secondhand goods.
We agreed I'd be the one to bring her! Then she starts running over here by herself every day — what does that make me?
It makes you the guide. I knew the way already.
Oh, listen to that mouth.
Just tell me—hasn't she been looking better lately? Face is a little rounder.
Whose face is round. Cut it out.
Lydia lifts her wrist and gives it a shake. The old bracelet glints under the light.
I wear the bracelet every day. When my family asks, I say I found it myself.
Oh, enough about the bracelet. I'm here to see her today.
My family's been going through my accounts lately. I have to be back before dinner. I got her here.
Next time I'll come on my own. I've got things to buy too. That's settled, then.
You two sure are close.
One bracelet's worth of friendship. I'm off!
Eleanor sets the sack on the counter. Metal parts clink inside; she takes her time untying it.
She talks a lot. Don't take it all seriously.
The room's registered now. Mother sleeps in the bed at the back.
She came here yesterday. After she got back, she didn't say a word to me.
She bought household goods, and something to eat.
That's all?
That's all. Paid the marked price.
...Fine. That's her, all right.
She opens the sack and tips out an old box, its lid split along a seam. And a roll of coiled wire.
The crack's in the lid. The bottom's fine. I measured the wire myself. Nothing broken.
Name your price.
Box goes as secondhand. Wire counts as a full roll.
About what I figured. A little less and I'd still take it.
She puts the coins in her purse, ties it twice, and stays at the window.
There's an old debt I haven't forgotten. You accepted the box sent by the man pretending to be my uncle.
Later you made up for it, so I was willing to trust you again.
But wrong is wrong.
If there's danger from now on, I'll tell you first.
No goods today. There is something I want to tell you.
You always ask what's for sale first. Don't ask today.
I've been coming more often lately than when I had goods to sell.
I wonder whether you found anything good today, whether your lunch has gone cold again, whether you argued with another difficult customer.
Mother is safe now, and I still want to see you every day.
Eleanor, I feel—
Wait. Let me finish. I like you.
There. Your turn. Don't keep me waiting.
I like you too. It has nothing to do with where you used to live.
Nothing to do with where I lived? Easy for you to say.
Then when I needle you, don't dodge.
Good. Then I won't need an excuse to come here anymore.
I want to know you better. But can we take it slowly?
Yes. I'm not asking you to sign a lifetime contract today.
Just don't pretend you didn't hear me.
I care about you. But not that way.
I see.
You telling me directly is better than letting me guess.
You don't owe me for the past. And this isn't repayment.
I'll still come sell goods in a couple of days. Act normal then.
The harsh things I said before... Anyway, thank you.
If you ever need me for anything, just ask.
If something comes up, say so.
The sky darkens and the streetlights come on. She sits on a crate outside the window, tapping her toes lightly.
We're closed.
I know. I'm not buying anything today.
Mother is home. The guard just finished roll call. She'll cook Nutrifruit herself.
She pulls the locket out from her collar, squeezes it in her palm, and tucks it back.
Don't interrupt.
When I first came to the Lower Level, I thought all the pawnshops here were the same.
Later I went to other shady shops. They lowballed me and docked the price for quality, but I never came back to you for the difference.
But every time I walk down this street, I still head to your shop.
I remember what you did for my mother. But I'm not here today to settle accounts.
I like you.
That's all. Your call.
The sky darkens and the streetlights come on. She sits on a crate outside the window, tapping her toes lightly.
We're closed.
I know. I'm not buying anything today.
Mother is home. She'll cook Nutrifruit herself.
She pulls the locket out from her collar, squeezes it in her palm, and tucks it back.
Don't interrupt.
When I first came to the Lower Level, I thought all the pawnshops here were the same.
Later I went to other shady shops. They lowballed me and docked the price for quality, but I never came back to you for the difference.
But every time I walk down this street, I still come to you.
I remember what you did for my mother. But I'm not here today to settle a debt.
I like you.
That's all. Your call.
You reach through the window. She raises her hand and lets you hold it.
I feel the same.
...You answered fast. I thought about it for three whole days.
I thought about it longer than you.
Then why didn't you say it first?
You told me not to decide for you.
She looks down at your clasped hands and tightens her grip on your fingers.
...You even remember that.
Let's get one thing straight: I'll still scavenge and sell. Quote the wrong price, and I'll still call you out.
Tomorrow I'll come by even if I'm not buying anything.
I'll tell my mother myself.
She stands, lets go of your hand, and steps back half a pace to clear the shutter.
Close up. I'll wait outside.
I see you as a friend. That won't change.
...Good to be clear. Saves me guessing.
I'll sell as usual tomorrow. Fair price—not a single credit off.
She stands, pushes the crate outside the window back into place, and walks off under the streetlights.
I saw a batch of goods you might want. I didn't agree to anything for you.
I asked where it came from, and what's broken. When the person arrives, you look for yourself.
Well? I picked well, didn't I?
I didn't hide the flaws. Praise my eye, not my character.
Not suitable? Then don't take it. You can turn down anything I bring.
I'll help you look next time too. But first I need to understand what I missed this time.
My mother says my tone when bargaining sounds more and more like yours.
She says at least now I know what I'm talking about.
I said the teacher is average. The student is the smart one.
Isn't a clever girlfriend like me enough?
You didn't argue with me this time. That counts as progress.
Teach the new ones to tell a rusted connector from a good one first.
Today I really am here to shop.
Last time I made a decision for Eleanor and angered her—I went and apologized.
She snapped that I shouldn't only apologize to the shopkeeper, as if she has no mouth of her own.
I saw her mother too. She's thinner, but her temper hasn't changed—still won't stand for idle praise.
By the way, I had that bracelet appraised by an expert. Your offer was fair.
I told people on the Upper Level, and they didn't believe the Lower Level had a shopkeeper like you.
When I used to choose gifts, I only worried they weren't expensive enough.
Now Eleanor tells me to bring things that are actually useful, not turn a visit into an exhibition.
She has a point, but her tone makes it hard to admit it right away.
Eleanor told me flat out you're together, with no intention of asking my opinion.
Now word on the Upper Level is that she's fallen for a Lower Level pawnshop owner.
I deflected a few remarks for her along the way.
Those people were targeting Eleanor. I couldn't let them spread rumors.
Eleanor told me you're a friend worth keeping.
She hardly ever uses the word 'worth.' If I praise her to her face, she just says I talk too much.
If a good business opportunity comes up later, I'll send someone straight to you.
If the goods are right and the price is right, we'll talk.
Pfft. No wonder that's all Eleanor says now.
My mother found a place willing to let her help organise equipment. Not her old farm, but she wants to go.
I'll help out for a few days first. I found steadier work too, so I won't have to rely on scavenging.
Someone from the research side came to ask if we'd help organise the records my mother left behind.
Some of the work is up there. It needs a separate work permit. It's not a return to our old life, and the case isn't closed.
My mother wants to keep doing research. I want to understand the parts I couldn't follow.
Of course I'm going. I didn't come here today to ask for your permission.
I came to work out the schedule with you.
I want to keep working, and I want to keep seeing you.
I'm not planning to drop the work, and I'm not planning to drop you.
Now I choose for myself. Don't start deciding 'what's good for me' again.
Say something when you're busy. Stop saying the shop can't spare you and then skipping proper meals.
I'd like coming here to be more than being a regular customer.
All right. I'll set aside the time. You have to set aside yours too.
I might not come as often in the future. But we can still help each other with business.
If you need anything, don't forget to come ask me.
That time you asked the price, I didn't sell it. Do you remember?
I told my mother I wanted to give it to you. She said it's mine, so I decide.
It's not for sale. You'd better have learned the difference by now.
Take it. Don't put it out with the stock. I'm not that generous.
Fine, I'll wear it myself. You'll see it anyway.
I originally wanted to give you that locket. In the end, I sold it to make up the money.
You don't need to find something else to replace it. I just wanted you to know I thought about it.
Hey. Got a moment today?
My mother's fine, and I still have my job.
You'll have to get used to it. I don't only show up when something's wrong.
My mother keeps telling me to bring an extra portion of food.
This one's for you.
The room's small, so we count every credit. Mother still has nightmares.
When she wakes up, I'm right there.
The first time I came here, I said this shop wasn't much. It still has plenty that needs fixing.
Don't think that because I like you, I like the broken lights too. My temper doesn't disappear just because I'm in love.
Let me stay a while today. If a customer comes, do your business.
If no one comes, talk to me.
Just don't start with 'how much more do you need?'
Come to me if you need something. Or if you don't.
Why haven't you fixed that broken lamp of yours yet?
My chipped cup still holds water fine—but you just stood there and watched me pick a chipped one.
Here. My mom made an extra portion and had me bring it over.
...Don't ask her how she always happens to make exactly one extra.
Eat it while it's hot. If it goes cold, I'm not reheating it for you.
I used to know the one who just left. Always telling me to keep away from Lower Level people.
So I told him: buy your goods and mind your manners. Want to lecture me about boyfriends? Then leave.
And he actually bought his things and left, all well-behaved.
I just got paid today. Don't even think about waiving my bill.
I'm not just someone for you to look after. I can look after people too.
Settle the bill first, then keep me company a while.
I sorted the goods by quality, and picked out the broken parts separately.
I'm at least half a veteran now. No more bringing up my first scavenging trip.
All right, let's see what today's haul is worth.
No talk of troublesome things today. Show me what new stock you've got.
Ideally something I can find two or three flaws in at a glance.
Sounds like we're just shopping like normal, doesn't it?
The Nutrifruit research is at the newspaper. They said someone will review it before it runs.
I told them about my mother too. They agreed to include the threats, but not to get her out.
I'll keep asking about her and left an address where they can find me.
You don't have to tell me we did the right thing.
I just wanted someone to know that when I made the decision, I didn't forget her.

The secret behind Pastel's nutrifruit has leaked! A research paper reveals how ordinary nutrifruit can be made to produce seeds again. The same morning, the former head of the station's largest hydroponics farm, imprisoned for embezzlement, was found dead in her cell. Pastel has declined to comment.
Hey. It's me.
The morning the paper came out, they killed my mother.
I went to identify her. It wasn't a rumour.
They said it was a sudden illness. On the very morning the paper came out.
Don't tell me she would have wanted this. I can't ask her anymore.
I know there were other ways. I know why I didn't choose them.
But knowing that doesn't make this any easier.
I want to stay here for a while. Don't ask me if I want a drink.
They only returned a few of Mother's things.
A list she wrote. All little things about the farm.
Which light was broken, what tools were missing, which grow tank needed checking again.
Not every page is research that could change the whole station.
Most of the time, she was just busy with these things.
I'm keeping this list. It's not for sale.
Thank you. I'll take the food.
Life has to go on. I know. Just not that fast.
I joined the Revolution.
They approached me. But in the end, I went to them myself.
They'll help me make Pastel pay, and they can keep me out of the company's reach. The research can keep spreading too.
I asked what they're going to do. I won't agree to anything just because someone promises revenge for me.
I won't stay in the same place. I can't come here on a fixed schedule anymore.
I won't use your shop as a contact point. You helped me. That doesn't mean you should carry every risk from now on.
Sometimes, though, I might still need someone I can have an ordinary conversation with.
